fields.Front: Why not connect every access ISP directly to every other access ISP?
fields.Back: It does not scale: with N access ISPs it needs O(N^2) connections.

fields.Text: Connecting millions of access ISPs pairwise needs {{c1::O(N^2)}} connections; instead each access ISP connects to a {{c2::global transit ISP}} under a {{c3::customer-provider}} economic agreement.
An {{c1::IXP (Internet exchange point)}} is a third-party meeting point where multiple ISPs can peer (connect directly to exchange traffic).

fields.Back: A direct connection between two ISPs (typically at the same level of the hierarchy) so traffic between them bypasses upstream providers; usually settlement-free (neither pays).

fields.Front: What role do regional ISPs play?
fields.Back: They arise to connect access networks within a region to the large (tier-1) ISPs, adding a tier to the hierarchy; access ISPs pay regional ISPs, regional ISPs pay tier-1 ISPs.

fields.Front: What are tier-1 ISPs? Give examples.
fields.Back: A small number of well-connected large commercial ISPs with national and international coverage that peer with each other and pay no one for transit; e.g., Level 3, Sprint, AT&T, NTT (roughly a dozen exist).

fields.Front: What is a content-provider network and why build one?
fields.Back: A private network (e.g., Google, Microsoft, Akamai, Facebook) connecting the provider's data centers to the Internet, bringing content close to users and often bypassing tier-1 and regional ISPs by peering directly with lower-tier ISPs or at IXPs.

fields.Text: At the 'center' of the Internet are a small number of {{c1::tier-1 commercial ISPs}} (e.g., Level 3, Sprint, AT&T, NTT) and {{c2::content provider networks}} (e.g., Google, Facebook).

fields.Front: What drove the evolution of the Internet's network-of-networks structure?
fields.Back: Economics and national policies, more than performance considerations.
